title: Job 7:1–7
context: The speaker is Job. Continuing his reply begun in chapter 6, he describes human life as hard service, like that of a hired laborer longing for evening and wages. His own lot is months of misery and wearisome nights; he tosses until dawn, his skin is diseased, and his days speed by without hope. By 7:7 he turns to address God directly, asking him to remember that his life is a breath. Job’s words are honest lament brought before God. Both traditions read them as genuine anguish within faith, not as a pattern to imitate in every detail, and Scripture’s willingness to give voice to such darkness has long comforted sufferers.

verses.text: “Isn’t a man forced to labor on earth? Aren’t his days like the days of a hired hand?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether human life on earth is not forced labor, like the days of a hired hand. Arminian readers see Job speaking for the hardship of human life in a world marked by toil and suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the image a frank account of life after the fall, compare Genesis 3:17–19 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read Job’s words as genuine lament, voiced from within his suffering.

verses.text: As a servant who earnestly desires the shadow, as a hireling who looks for his wages,
verses.arminianNotes: Like a servant longing for shade and a hireling waiting for wages, Job waits for relief. Arminian readers note that the longing is real, yet Job has no assurance of when or whether it will come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the images of servant and hireling as expressing weariness with labor that seems to bring no rest. Both traditions read the verse as a vivid comparison drawn from daily life in Job’s world.

verses.text: so I am made to possess months of misery, wearisome nights are appointed to me.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says he has been allotted months of misery and wearisome nights. Arminian readers note the passive language, made to possess and appointed, which shows Job feels his suffering is imposed on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job sensing that his suffering comes under God’s hand, though he does not understand why. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s honest account, not as a doctrinal statement about providence.

verses.text: When I lie down, I say, ‘When will I arise, and the night be gone?’ I toss and turn until the dawning of the day.
verses.arminianNotes: Lying down, Job longs for the night to end, tossing until dawn. Arminian readers see the sleeplessness of deep distress, and note that Scripture does not hide such nights from view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the verse the restlessness that suffering brings to body and mind. Both traditions read it pastorally: Job’s lament gives words to sufferers, and those in such nights are encouraged to seek care from others.

verses.text: My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust. My skin closes up, and breaks out afresh.
verses.arminianNotes: Job describes his flesh clothed with worms and dust, his skin breaking out again. Arminian readers note the physical suffering behind Job’s words, which the book does not soften.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the description as recalling the affliction of 2:7–8. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a raw portrait of bodily suffering, reported without explanation of its cause at this point in the book.

verses.text: My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, and are spent without hope.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says his days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle and spent without hope. Arminian readers see the image of rapid, unstoppable passing time, made worse by the loss of hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as expressing how suffering can make life seem both endless at night and brief overall. Both traditions read Job’s lack of hope as honest despair voiced to God, not as the book’s final word.

verses.text: Oh remember that my life is a breath. My eye will no more see good.
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks God to remember that his life is a breath and that he will see good no more. Arminian readers observe the shift in address: from here Job speaks to God in the second person, still reaching toward him while sure of nothing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal as an act of faith: Job still speaks to God, even when he feels abandoned. Shared ground: both traditions read the plea as honest lament within a relationship with God.
